newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian, Bosnian leaders meet Holbrooke.
newsitem.headline: Croatian, Bosnian leaders meet Holbrooke.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnia's presidency chairman, Alija Izetbegovic, met straight-talking U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who travelled to this Adriatic resort on Wednesday to try to boost the slow-moving Balkan peace process.

The two leaders issued a statement afterward pledging to co-operate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal, to protect refugees returning to their homes and to set up proper border controls between Croatia and Bosnia.

Holbrooke, the architect of a peace agreement that ended four years of war in former Yugoslavia, expressed caution over Wednesday's agreement which essentially reiterated obligations set out under the peace treaty.
He told reporters the real test would be in carrying out the agreement.
"Let's see what happens. We have made very clear that when parties make commitments we expect them to meet them. If they don't carry them out there will be penalties," Holbrooke said.
The American diplomat timed his return to the Balkans to coincide with the summit and will later travel to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo and to the Yugoslav capital Belgrade.
His visit comes amid mounting international pressure to move the stalled Bosnian peace process forward.

The joint statement indicated that Tudjman's government might be willing to turn over sensitive defence documents demanded by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, which is currently trying a Bosnian Croat militia officer.
"President Tudjman will do his utmost to effect the transfer or voluntary surrender of Croat indictees currently at large to the tribunal on an urgent basis," the statement said.
"Croatia will also co-operate in providing documents requested by the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia."
Zagreb has refused so far to hand over documents requested by the tribunal and has turned a blind eye to indicted fugitives residing in Croatia or Croat-controlled areas in Bosnia.
Robert Gelbard, the U.S. envoy to Bosnia who accompanied Holbrooke, said that Washington expected the parties to fulfil their pledges on the war criminals issue "quickly".
"We didn't set a deadline yet but we expect them to act urgently. It's not a year, it's not six months, it means quickly," Gelbard said.

Tudjman and Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic have been criticised for failing to hand over suspected war criminals to The Hague, though Tudjman contends he has done more than Milosevic given their countries' respective roles in the war.

Tudjman has also come under intense international lobbying to strengthen his support of the Moslem-Croat Federation, formed in 1994 with the help of U.S. diplomacy, which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the Bosnian presidency, earlier told reporters that the pace at which refugee returns could be achieved had been overestimated.
"I think we had overestimated the possibility of implementing something like the return of refugees, freedom of movement and punishment of war criminals," Izetbegovic said.

Tudjman and Izetbegovic condemned recent violence and harassment of Moslem refugees trying to return to central Bosnia and Serb refugees moving back to Sarajevo. The two leaders promised prompt investigations and prosecution of those responsible.
Over the weekend hundreds of Moslem refugees fled their homes in the town of Jajce under intimidation from angry, drunken Bosnian Croat mobs.
They had moved back to their pre-war homes in the area in recent weeks and said after leaving that they would try to return once again.
Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the presidency, and Tudjman have had stormy relations since leading their republics out of the old Yugoslav federation.
Tudjman was anxious to hold the meeting earlier to prove to the United States and Europe that he supported the Federation.

But Izetbegovic had declined to meet Tudjman for months until Zagreb made good on previous commitments. Tudjman pushed Croats in the divided town of Mostar into agreeing to a unified police force last month, clearing the way for the talks.
